lessons.title: Equipment on an aquaculture farm
lessons.html:
Know your equipment

Fish farms depend on equipment running day and night. A failed aerator or pump at 02:00 can kill a whole tank before morning. A supervisor must know what each item does, how it fails and how to keep it running.

Water supply and movement

  • Pumps: centrifugal and submersible pumps move water from boreholes, dams and sumps.
  • Pipework, valves and plumbing: control flow to each unit; leaks waste water and power.
  • Screens: on inlets and outlets keep wild fish and debris out and farm fish in.

Aeration and oxygen

  • Paddlewheel aerators are common in earth ponds.
  • Air blowers and diffusers supply air to tanks.
  • Oxygen cones and pure oxygen are used in intensive systems; oxygen cylinders must be handled as pressurised gas.

Recirculating system equipment

  • Mechanical filters (drum filters, settling tanks) remove solids.
  • Biofilters host bacteria that convert ammonia.
  • UV units reduce pathogens in the water.
  • Heaters or heat pumps where warm-water species are grown in cold areas.

Husbandry and harvest equipment

  • Seine nets, scoop nets, graders, baskets, crates and bins.
  • Scales for weighing samples and harvests.
  • Transport tanks with aeration.
  • Feeders: hand scoops, demand feeders, automatic feeders.

Monitoring and power

  • DO, temperature and pH meters, and test kits.
  • Alarms that warn of low oxygen, low water level or power failure.
  • Standby generators, which are essential given load shedding and rural power outages in South Africa.

Keep an equipment register listing each item, its location, serial number, supplier, date bought and service schedule.

Keep spare parts for critical items on site: aerator motors or paddles, pump seals, fuses, diffuser heads and net repair twine. A missing R200 part can otherwise cause losses worth many thousands of rand while a supplier is found.

lessons.title: Maintenance, safety and records
lessons.html:
Planned maintenance

Breakdown repairs cost more than planned care. Set daily, weekly and monthly checks for each item.

FrequencyExample checks
DailyAerators running, pumps primed, screens clear, alarms armed, oxygen supply level
WeeklyClean filters and diffusers, check nets for holes, run generator under load
MonthlyLubricate bearings and gearboxes per manual, check belts, inspect cables and earth leakage
Annually or as manual saysPump and motor service, calibration by supplier

Standby and redundancy

Critical systems need backup: spare aerators, a spare pump, enough fuel for the generator and an oxygen reserve. Test backup equipment on a schedule, not only when it is needed.

Safety

  • Electricity and water: use earth leakage protection, keep connections dry and off the ground, and allow only qualified electricians to do electrical work.
  • Lockout: isolate and lock out power before cleaning or repairing pumps and aerators so nobody can switch them on.
  • Rotating parts: paddlewheels and belts must have guards; never reach in while they run.
  • Generators: run outdoors or in ventilated areas because exhaust gas can kill; store fuel safely away from heat.
  • Oxygen cylinders: secure upright, keep oil and grease away, no smoking or flames nearby.
  • Chemicals for cleaning and disinfection: follow the label and safety data sheet.

The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 requires the employer to provide and maintain safe machinery and to train workers in safe use.

Cleaning and biosecurity

Nets, graders and transport tanks move between units and farms and carry disease. Clean off organic matter first, then disinfect, then dry. Keep separate equipment for quarantine units.

Records and replacement

Log every service, fault and repair with date, cost and who did it. Repeated failures show when an item should be replaced. Use these records when budgeting.

Key points

  • Keep an equipment register with service schedules.
  • Do daily checks on aerators, pumps, screens and alarms.
  • Test standby generators and backup aeration regularly.
  • Lock out power before working on equipment.
  • Clean, disinfect and dry equipment that moves between units.

options.text: Power cuts can stop aeration and pumps and kill fish
They are required for weighing fish

quiz.question: What must be done before repairing a pump?

options.text: Isolate and lock out the power

quiz.question: Where should a generator be run?

options.text: Outdoors or in a well-ventilated area

quiz.question: What is the correct order for cleaning nets between units?

Dry, then disinfect, then rinse in pond water
Disinfect only, no need to clean
